articles.title_orig: As war strains Kremlin finances, Putin reaches into more pockets in search of new revenue streams
articles.title_zh: As war strains Kremlin finances, Putin reaches into more pockets in search of new revenue streams
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
With Russia’s invasion of Ukraine intensifying the strain on state finances, President Vladimir Putin is reaching for cash to fund his government and the war, squeezing tax revenue from an economy that’s increasingly skewed toward the military — while civilian needs take a back seat.
The country's 2027-2029 state budget, which will be taken up Thursday in the rubber-stamp parliament, is accompanied by a string of tax hikes announced after the September parliamentary elections.
While last year the Kremlin went for a broad tax increase, raising value-added taxes at the cash register and making more small businesses pay VAT , this cash grab hits a narrower segment: mining companies and better-off citizens with investment income, property sales and bank accounts.
The budget deficit this year has swelled beyond forecast s due to lavish military spending and tepid economic growth amid sanctions, high interest rates for non-military companies, labor shortages and Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and export terminals.
The deficit hit 5.8 trillion rubles ($72 billion) through August, almost 50% higher than last year's figure and above the already revised target of 4.8 trillion rubles, according to the Kyiv School of Economics.
New taxes will hit mining companies and bank interest
The government proposes a 20%-30% windfall profits tax on mining companies that have benefited from prices that have risen since last year. That will hit companies producing iron ore, nickel and gold. Another measure imposes higher rates of 13% to 22% on income from interest, dividends and proceeds from selling property. Such income is currently taxed at 13% for amounts under 2.4 million rubles ($29,800) and 15% above that.
Other proposals to take effect Jan. 1 include a 100-ruble per parcel charge and 22% VAT on formerly tax-free foreign goods worth less than 200 euros that are bought online. There's also a 35% tax on dividends paid into restricted accounts for foreign investors from “unfriendly countries."
People asked about taxes and finances on the street in Moscow responded with a mix of complaints and resignation. "They need money for state coffers, they need to collect more from people, from ordinary people,” said Denis Bystrov, 39.
“What can you do?” said Nelly Godunova, 92. “I've got four university degrees, they were all free, you know? True, I've given plenty to this country. But no matter... If you earned something, you've got to give back.”
“Everyone knows perfectly well that the money's going for the military operation, right?” said Sergei Sukachev, who gave his age as “almost 70.” “I've suffered a little as a businessman, to be honest, but I clearly understand, it's best to hang on and to get our way.”
Russia is not facing a financial crisis, but a long-term erosion of public welfare
Russia has enough financing available to cover the deficit in 2027 and probably 2028, says Chris Weafer, CEO of consultancy Macro-Advisory Ltd. “But that is at the expense of raising taxes, of increasing costs for households as well as business,” he said.
“And it means that there is much less money available for normal economic development or infrastructure. Basically, the budget is now moving to a phase where it is primarily funding the military and the military operation.”
“So the economy is now becoming very skewed,” he said. "While there’s still modest positive growth, it is coming from the state spending into these ... state-linked industries, whereas the rest of the economy is struggling badly or even failing.”
German company Russian subsidiary looted for a billion rubles
A subsidiary of German retailer Metro was seized under a law permitting the temporary administration of firms from “unfriendly countries” and tapped for a billion-ruble ($12 million) contribution to the war effort.
Metro AG headquarters in Germany said it had no role in the donation, which “does not reflect our position or the way we run our business.”
Metro Russia, no longer under the control of headquarters, said the contribution to the “National Front - Everything for Victory” fund would buy vehicles, communications devices and anti-drone equipment for soldiers in what Russia calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.
Weafer said Russia may be seizing control of foreign companies in anticipation of a deal to secure Russian assets frozen abroad. But the forced donation also raises the risk that the Finance Ministry may see foreign companies as sources of windfall revenue.
Russia's limited sources of financing are being squeezed
Russia's economic numbers don't look that bad — on the surface. The government predicts growth this year of 0.6% of GDP , not great but not a recession either. Unemployment is at a record low, and the government carries very little debt. Earnings from oil exports have held up thanks to higher global prices caused by the war in Iran. The revised deficit for this year will come in around 3% of GDP, according to Finance Minister Anton Siluanov. That is more than the 1.6% achieved last year, but smaller than in many other countries. For instance, the US booked 5.8% of GDP last year. Russia is roughly equal to the EU average of 3.1%.
But that isn't the whole story. Due to sanctions that forbid banks and investors from dealing with Russia, the Kremlin can’t tap international bond markets. And Russia's domestic financial resources have already been extensively drawn down.
One way is to borrow from Russian banks through bond sales. But that came under stress this summer when banks balked at the low interest rate. Sales resumed after the government offered better terms. The government has already tapped the banking system by having banks fund the war with loans to defense companies, shifting the true costs of the war off the federal budget and onto the balance sheets of banks and state-controlled companies, according to the Kyiv School of Economics.
Another pot is the National Wealth Fund, a reserve built up from oil and gas export earnings. But the fund's liquid assets available for spending, such as Chinese currency and gold, have dwindled to 1.7% of GDP.
The Kyiv School of Economics says that Russia's finances are stable -- for the moment.
But “the room for maneuver is limited: an adverse shock such as a drop in global energy prices or an erosion of confidence in the financial system could quickly destabilize the fragile equilibrium.”

articles.title_orig: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.title_zh: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.content_orig:
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

articles.title_orig: Earnings live updates: Eli Lilly stock pops as strong GLP-1 drug demand lifts results, ServiceNow stock plunges
articles.title_zh: Earnings live updates: Eli Lilly stock pops as strong GLP-1 drug demand lifts results, ServiceNow stock plunges
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Third quarter earnings season is in full swing this week, with corporate results dropping from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
Read more: Follow Microsoft earnings live updates here.
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals will be represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also open their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
Caterpillar ( CAT ) reported and a record order backlog of $78.1 billion in the third quarter, but the stock fell 11% in premarket trading as Wall Street set a high bar and AI-related stocks broadly got hit.
The company has become a growing industrial AI play as its power generation business, which makes and services turbines, has gotten a boost amid booming data center construction.
Here's what Caterpillar reported, versus analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: increased 17% to $20.7 billion, in line with Wall Street estimates.
Adjusted earnings per share: $7.20, versus estimates of $7.03 per share.
Guidance: Maintained full-year outlook for sales to grow in the mid-to-high teens
Analysts may be down on the stock as they were hoping for raised guidance and a wider sales beat.
"Our third-quarter results reflect the durability of our end markets, with strong order rates and a record backlog," Caterpillar CEO Joe Creed said in the release. "Our team continues to execute our strategic priorities in a dynamic environment, positioning us for a strong year while delivering long-term value for our customers and shareholders."
Eli Lilly ( LLY ) shares jumped 4% in premarket trading as strong demand for the company's GLP-1 drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound boosted the company's third quarter results.
Here's what Eli Lilly reported, versus analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: up 39% year over year to $24.4 billion, versus estimates of $22.6 billion
Adjusted earnings per share: up 7% to $7.48, versus estimates of $6.35
Guidance: Increased full-year revenue guidance to a new range of $91 billion to $92 billion
"Revenue growth was driven by broad global consumer demand for Mounjaro and Zepbound, the global launches of Foundayo, expanded U.S. coverage for obesity care and a doubling in our newest products in oncology, immunology and neuroscience," Lilly CEO David Ricks said in the earnings release.
Mounjaro sales rose 65% year over year to $10.7 billion, while Zepbound sales were up 49% to $5.35 billion.
Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) profit took a hit from an unusual place: its stakes in other companies.
Those holdings include about 14% of Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ). They supplied about $6 of Alphabet's $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter. In the third quarter, a nearly $9 billion loss on them cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12.
The filing that shows which stakes fell isn't out yet, but SpaceX stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.
Watch Anthropic's IPO, which could start trading as soon as Nov. 16. Once it's public, Alphabet will value that stake at the market price every quarter.
Chipotle ( CMG ) reported third quarter earnings on Wednesday after market close that were better than the Street expected as the restaurant chain sustained sales momentum following slower sales growth since the first quarter of 2025.
Chipotle posted a 2.1% gain in same-store sales, higher than the 1.5% gain Wall Street expected. It posted adjusted earnings of $0.27 per share, slightly below the $0.29 per share expected.
"Three consecutive quarters of positive comparable transaction growth demonstrates that our Recipe for Growth strategy is working," CEO Scott Boatwright wrote in the release, adding that the company saw traction around its menu and digital innovation, high-efficiency equipment rollout and global expansion.
The stock rose 2%. Year to date, shares are down 20%.
ServiceNow ( NOW ) stock plunged 15% after the company missed earnings expectations.
Here's what the enterprise software company reported in Q3, versus analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: $4.1 billion, versus estimates of $4.09 billion
Earnings per share: $0.27, versus estimates of $0.35 per share
Current remaining performance obligations (cRPO): $13.65 billion, representing 20.5% year-over-year growth
Guidance: ServiceNow raised its forecast for 2026 subscription revenues to $15.78 billion to $15.79 billion.
"This was more than another beat-and-raise quarter for ServiceNow, this was the inflection point for ServiceNow as the Super Intelligence Control Tower," CEO Bill McDermott said in the earnings release. "Our customers have validated our strategic relevance as the single harness for enterprise intelligence and security."
Yahoo Finance's Daniel Howley reports:
Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) reported its third quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, missing revenue projections on lower-than-anticipated advertising sales.
Google saw earnings per share (EPS) of $2.12 on revenue of 127.58 billion. Analysts were looking for EPS of $3.01 on revenue of $127.93 billion. Revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs came in at $111.21 billion. Wall Street was anticipating $111.29 billion.
Google's advertising segment saw sales of $82.01 billion versus expectations of $83.5 billion, while its cloud unit brought in $30.71 billion. Analysts were projecting revenue of $29.1 billion.
The results come just hours after the company debuted its latest frontier AI model.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
Ford ( F ) reported third quarter earnings that topped estimates and upped the lower end of its profit guidance. The company still sees EV losses piling up by the end of the year.
For the quarter, Ford reported automotive revenue of $46.1 billion vs. $46.2 billion, per Bloomberg consensus, with adjusted EPS of $0.49 vs. $0.41, and adjusted EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) of $2.66 billion vs. $2.38 billion.
Ford tightened the low end of its full-year adjusted EBIT guidance to between $10.5 billion and $11 billion (from $10 billion to $11 billion seen prior); analysts projected full-year adjusted EBIT of $10.52 billion. Ford's adjusted free cash flow guidance remained at $6 billion to $7 billion.
Vertiv ( VRT ) stock surged 15% in premarket trading as the data center infrastructure player showed it continues to benefit from the massive capex spending from the likes of Google ( GOOG ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ).
"We are in the middle of the largest infrastructure buildout and it's accelerating," Vertiv's CEO Giordano Albertazzi said. "The demands on data center infrastructure are evolving faster than ever, and Vertiv's role in that buildout keeps expanding."
Vertiv makes power and cooling hardware for data centers and enterprise networks. As AI fuels demand for this infrastructure, Vertiv said its orders have doubled year over year. The company counts Alphabet, Microsoft, Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) among its customers, per S&P Global Market Intelligence.
That demand, plus strong third quarter results, have given Vertiv the confidence to raise its full-year outlook. In 2026, the company expects net sales of $14.45 billion to $14.85 billion, up from $13.8 billion to $14.2 billion.
Adjusted diluted earnings per share are expected to be $7.10-$7.20 for the year, representing earnings growth of 69%-71%. The midpoint of that range is above the $6.73 per share forecast Wall Street analysts penciled in.
In the third quarter, Vertiv reported net sales of $4.31 billion, beating Wall Street's expectations of $3.76 billion. Adjust

articles.title_orig: Decommissioned NVIDIA supercomputer with 9,600 A100 GPUs hits eBay for $60 million, free shipping included
articles.title_zh: Decommissioned NVIDIA supercomputer with 9,600 A100 GPUs hits eBay for $60 million, free shipping included
articles.content_orig:
An IT hardware reseller has listed a decommissioned NVIDIA AI supercomputer on eBay for $59.7 million, or best offer. The seller, Core 4 Solutions, is offering 300 server racks containing 9,600 NVIDIA A100 accelerators and 4,200 AMD EPYC processors. And yes, the listing includes free FedEx Ground shipping. Buyers in a hurry can even select overnight delivery for just $50.
The hardware comes from a decommissioned hyperscaler environment and uses NVIDIA A100 40GB SXM4 accelerators based on the Ampere architecture introduced in 2020. Each rack contains four compute nodes with eight GPUs each, alongside management systems and networking equipment. The complete configuration includes 268,800 Zen 2 CPU cores, 384TB of GPU memory and approximately 1.4PB of combined system memory.
At $59.7 million, the asking price is equivalent to nearly 29,865 GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards at NVIDIA’s official $1,999 MSRP . Or closer to 7500 units at current prices. Of course, this comparison is purely financial, since the A100 is a data center accelerator rather than a gaming GPU. The asking price works out to approximately $6,219 per A100, although that also covers the processors, memory, networking hardware and server racks. The seller also offers individual 32-GPU racks for $199,000.
The bulk listing has since ended with the item marked as no longer available, although there is no confirmation that a sale took place.

articles.title_orig: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 passengers, mostly Americans, are stranded in Cambodia after the operator of a luxury U.S. cruise ship that was on a continuous around-the-world voyage ran out of money due to skyrocketing fuel costs .
Villa Vie Residences, the Florida-based operator of the MV Odyssey, said the war with Iran quadrupled fuel costs and forced it to suspend operations on Tuesday.
CEO Mikael Petterson told CBS News in a phone interview Wednesday that Villa Vie Residences was paying an average of $700 a ton for fuel before the war broke out in late February. Since then, it has been paying anywhere from $2,000 to $3,000 per ton.
The Odyssey uses between 700 and 800 tons per month in fuel, Petterson disclosed.
"When you divide it over 300 people on board, it's just backbreaking," Petterson told CBS News. "And this has been going on for nine months. We've tried to do everything we can do."
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said the per cabin fuel costs rose from an average of $1,800 per month before the war to between $6,000 and $8,000.
The company was unwilling to pass those rising costs on to its passengers, Petterson said.
The Odyssey launched in October 2024 for a continuous around-the-world journey. At the time, passengers could become residents of the ship by purchasing a permanent cabin for several hundred thousand dollars. Some sold their homes to do so. At the time, they were given a 15-year minimum guarantee of residency aboard the Odyssey.
The Odyssey attempted to counter the spiking fuel prices by slowing down its itinerary and spending five or six days in each port "hoping that things would come to a close in the Middle East," Petterson said, but it wasn't enough.
"For us, when our monthly expenses go up from $400,000 to $2 million, where are we going to get the $1.6 million?" Petterson asked.
The Villa Vie Residences CEO said that the ship ran out of money as it searched for a financial partner, and the plan is now to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
"We've borrowed money, we've stretched our payrolls as far as we can, and we're at a point where it's just at a breaking point where we need capitalization," Petterson said.
Passenger Benjamin Schatz thought the MV Odyssey would be his forever home.
"Honestly, right now, I'm in denial and in shock, and I'm heartbroken," Schatz, a retiree, told CBS News.
CBS News met Schatz in April 2025 for a story featuring Villa Vie Residences. At that point, he had been living on the ship for about one year. On Wednesday, he was given just hours to pack up his life and leave.
Said Schatz: "There are people now who are homeless and who have very little money and don't know what they're going to do."

articles.title_orig: Popular airline hits customers with steep fee hike for first time in 8 years
articles.title_zh: Popular airline hits customers with steep fee hike for first time in 8 years
articles.content_orig:
The Points Guy editor Nick Ewen breaks down American Airlines' upcoming credit card changes, including higher annual fees and additional benefits.
The era of the standard $99 airline credit card may be fading as American Airlines becomes the latest major carrier to adjust its price tag.
Beginning Jan. 24, 2027, the annual fee for both the Citi/AAdvantage Platinum Select MasterCard and the Citi/AAdvantage Business MasterCard will jump from $99 to $150, according to a company press release.
The adjustment marks the first price hike for the popular Platinum Select consumer card since 2018, signaling a shift in the travel rewards landscape.
MAJOR AIRLINE DITCHES SNACKS DURING SHORT FLIGHTS AS ‘ZERO SERVICE’ SPARKS DEBATE
To soften the blow of a nearly 52% fee increase, American Airlines, Citi and MasterCard are adding several new travel and lifestyle perks.
Whether those additions make up for the $51 increase will depend largely on how travelers use the card, Nick Ewen, editor-in-chief of The Points Guy, told Fox News Digital.
"You have to look at the real dollar value based on your own travel habits," said Ewen, who is based in Florida.
American Airlines customers with select Citi/AAdvantage credit cards will see their annual fees rise from $99 to $150 beginning Jan. 24, 2027. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
Cardholders will gain additional ways to earn AAdvantage miles on everyday spending, along with up to $120 toward Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years, American Airlines confirmed.
Additionally, a new $100 annual statement credit for in-flight purchases will replace the previous 25% food and beverage discount.
This makes the card significantly more rewarding for travelers, as the credit can be applied toward broad in-flight expenses, including Wi-Fi, which was explicitly excluded under the old discount system.
"You may not be able to stomach that additional increased annual fee."
For someone who regularly spends money aboard American flights or already pays for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, Ewen said the new credits could help offset the higher annual fee.
"If the answer is yes, you're definitely going to come out ahead," he said of travelers who typically spend up to $100 on in-flight purchases each year.
PASSENGER JET BOUND FOR US PLUNGES 27,000 FEET BEFORE CIRCLING FOR HOURS
The changes may not be for everyone, however.
"If you're only flying American once a year, you may not be able to stomach that additional increased annual fee," he said.
Some travelers are wondering whether the added benefits will justify the higher annual fees. (iStock)
The changes also include adjustments to how cardholders can rack up rewards on everyday purchases, according to the press release.
The personal Platinum Select card will offer three miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and Cars bookings and two miles per dollar on gas and EV charging , select streaming services, and eligible Rides and Rails purchases.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Existing perks — including preferred boarding, no foreign transaction fees and a free first checked bag on domestic American itineraries for the cardholder and up to four companions — will remain intact.
Ewen said the higher fee follows a broader shift among airline rewards cards.
"American is far from the first airline that we've seen this increase in their annual fees," he said, pointing to similar changes from Delta, Southwest and United.
American Airlines' credit card changes come amid a broader industry trend of airline rewards cards moving toward annual fees of approximately $150. (Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images)
Entry-level airline cards that once hovered around $100 annually are increasingly moving closer to $150, Ewen said.
"This is definitely the norm, although it's not universal across the board," he added.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
The move by American Airlines aligns with a broader trend sweeping the credit card sector.
Over the past few years, the travel rewards market has seen steady fee inflation as issuers pack mid-tier and premium cards with statement credits and subscription services.
The move by American Airlines aligns with a broader trend sweeping the credit card sector.
Financial institutions are betting consumers will accept higher upfront costs in exchange for tangible, use-it-or-lose-it perks, transforming traditional flight-focused credit cards into broader lifestyle products, according to reports.
The changes drew mixed reactions from cardholders online.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Call me crazy, but none of this is an upgrade," one Reddit user commented.
Another questioned the value of the new in-flight credit .
To soften the blow of a 52% fee increase, American Airlines, Citi and MasterCard are adding several new travel and lifestyle perks. (Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"These inflight credit[s] [are] annoying," the person wrote. "They don't even stock them except for longer flights."
Others were more receptive to the new benefits, with one commenter pointing to the Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit as a reason the higher fee could be worthwhile.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
"This has become more of a respectable airline card in my opinion now with this refresh," one user wrote.
Kelly McGreal is a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. She and the team cover travel, food and drink, health, relationships and more. She also produces the weekly American Culture Quiz and handles other special projects.

articles.title_orig: EasySMX S10 Lite Review: A Switch 2 Fidget Toy With A Weird Removable Faceplate
articles.title_zh: EasySMX S10 Lite Review: A Switch 2 Fidget Toy With A Weird Removable Faceplate
articles.content_orig:
EasySMX is using Elizabeth Holmes levels of pedantry with this faceplate situation.
Of all the Switch 2 controllers I've reviewed in 2026, this is probably the most unexpected pick. EasySMX isn't as well-known as 8BitDo or Turtle Beach, and the S10 Lite is its most pared-down Switch 2 gamepad, regularly listed for $40. The price is exactly what intrigued me about the S10 Lite in the first place, considering most Switch 2 controllers cost around $70, and Nintendo's own Pro Controller is $90. A feature-rich gamepad that can potentially compete with 8BitDo's incredible, $30 Ultimate 2C ? I'm here for it.
And then just as swiftly, I'm gone. While the EasySMX S10 Lite has supremely tactile buttons, Hall effect sticks with a soft-hit feel, motion controls and strong haptics, it also has a semi-transparent, magnetically attached faceplate that's so wonky and cheap-feeling that it overshadows the controller's more attractive features. I'm someone who tends to enjoy oddball ideas in my gaming accessories and I can't fully make sense of the S10 Lite faceplate. The way that EasySMX has chosen to market this removable piece of plastic, using misleading verbiage around the availability of custom options, has only poured fuel on the confusion fire.
First, the basics and the good bits. The EasySMX S10 Lite is indeed light and compact, with a creamy plastic finish along the body and an anti-slip diamond texture on the backs of the grips. There are two buttons on the rear of the controller, mappable by pressing and holding a small nearby input marked M. I wish the rear buttons crept up the sides of the grips more, allowing my fingertips to more comfortably hit them, but they're certainly within reach and nice to have. The S10 Lite comes in two colors, ice blue or pastel pink, and while the pink is clearly the cuter option, they're both charming.
There are some fabulous modern features built into the S10 Lite, including precise, anti-drift Hall effect analog sticks that hit the sides of their enclosures silently and super softly. The sound and feel is comparable to Nintendo's proprietary soft-hit action on the Pro Controller, which is a notable feat. That said, the stick click on the S10 Lite is a little too stiff for my liking, and it does make an audible pop when pressed. I'm not personally complaining about the noise, which I find soothing on an ASMR level, but it's notable when the sticks themselves are so darn pillowy otherwise.
The face buttons are tactile microswitches with a wonderfully clicky sound and feel. However, they're also fairly rigid, especially compared with something like the springy mechanical buttons on Razer's Wolverine V3 Pro (my personal favorite gamepad, though it only supports PC and Xbox, and also costs an eye-watering $200. See? I told you the price point was appealing here). The haptics in the S10 Lite are nice and strong, with four intensity settings, and at most they make a slight whining sound rather than grinding.
The bumpers and wide-flared triggers stand out prominently from the chassis, and the triggers have a clicky microswitch action like the face buttons. While I do adore fidget-toy features in my controllers — and the S10 Lite definitely delivers on this point — in-game, I prefer a smooth and sensitive Hall effect pull in the triggers. It's a tradeoff between satisfying sounds and modern comfort that you'll have to consider for yourself.
I like that the home, GameChat and capture buttons are lined up at the bottom of the controller's face, separate from the plus and minus inputs in the center of the pad. This configuration should reduce the number of random, accidental screenshots that you end up taking while trying to quickly open the inventory in Resident Evil Requiem or peep the menu in Hello Kitty Island Adventure , for completely random example.
The S10 Lite has nine-axis motion controls and a Turbo function that allows you to set input macros to a simple button combo. It's also able to wake up the Switch 2 from afar, one of the raddest features a controller can have. The quick-start card that's included in the box is actually helpful in terms of connecting the gamepad to the console. And what's more, there's a built-in toggle on the backside of the pad that lets you swap between Switch and Switch 2 compatibility, or PC, Android and iOS play. In the box, you get the gamepad, a charging cable and the instruction card.
The gamepad, of course, includes the faceplate, attached with four visible, circular magnets and some tension. When I pulled my S10 Lite out of the box, the bottom ridge of the faceplate wasn't fully tucked into place, raised in a way that was mildly infuriating but not clearly unintentional. It wasn't until I was fidgeting with the controller, waiting for a game to download, that I realized I could pop in the transparent-blue plastic so it sat flat along the bottom. Even still, the left side of my faceplate refuses to depress as deeply as the right, so there's a sliver of icy plastic peering over one grip, catching my fingertips and compelling me to pick at it. I may be able to adjust this by tightening a tiny screw on that side, but all things considered, I'd rather not have to.
This leads us to the obvious question: Why have a removable faceplate in the first place? It would make sense if EasySMX had, say, a marketplace of cute alternatives that anyone could purchase and swap into their own pad, allowing the brand to jump on trends and collaborate with cool creators, naturally extending the money-making potential of the S10 Lite. That would make perfect sense. But that's not what EasySMX is doing.
The controller's product page provides just one sentence about faceplates, reading, "DIY Your Controller: express your personality with DIY Magnetic Faceplates & Stickers, allowing you to swap covers instantly to match your mood or your favorite game theme." Those first three letters are doing the heavy lifting, since EasySMX doesn't actually sell replacement or custom faceplates of any kind. The only way to guarantee you'll get one is to make it yourself, but even then, it appears that 3D files and high-quality images of the faceplates aren't publicly available . The company also doesn't sell stickers, an additional accessory it mentions without prompting.
With this context in mind, it's unclear what EasySMX means by DIY Your Controller , but it feels like a purposefully misleading, weaselly turn of phrase — like Elizabeth Holmes saying to Nathan Fielder, "You can see everything."
EasySMX does hold giveaways for customized faceplates on Reddit and Discord every now and then, it seems, but these are scattered. It's possible that the company is gathering data and ramping up to produce faceplates that players can buy, but right now, they're weirdly unattainable.
I really like tactile buttons, soft-hit sticks and the idea of modular art on my controller, but I really, really hate being lied to, and it kinda feels like that's what EasySMX is doing with the faceplate situation. The EasySMX S10 Lite is fine for kids (or adults) who love a good click and don't mind a messy faceplate, but otherwise, this thing is never beating the 8BitDo Ultimate 2C in terms of affordability and features.

articles.title_orig: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.
The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.
In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.
Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.
Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.
All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.
Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.
The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.
Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.
Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s election rhetoric: What candidates said, and how they performed
articles.title_zh: Israel’s election rhetoric: What candidates said, and how they performed
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s parliamentary election on Tuesday produced no clear winner, with nearly 90 percent of ballots counted and both major political blocs falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc is on course to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is expected to secure 48 seats.
The Arab-majority parties won 19 seats, a historic high, driven by record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel of about 80 percent. That has placed the Arab parties at the centre of coalition arithmetic, even as several party leaders ruled out governing with them.
So what did the main contenders say in the run-up to and during the vote, and how did they fare? Here is a look:
Pre-election: In the build-up to the election, Netanyahu expressed confidence, telling The Jerusalem Post on October 22, “I’m gonna have five more terms.”
On Sunday, he targeted the opposition, with Haaretz citing a broadcast on Israel’s Channel 14 that Netanyahu warned if they win, they will “give citizenship to hundreds of thousands of Palestinians”, a move that would signal the “end of the Jewish state”.
Election day: On Tuesday, he said forming a government with Arab-led parties would be “a shame and a disgrace”.
“It is forbidden – simply forbidden – to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he told supporters.
Post-election day: After the elections, Netanyahu’s Likud party took aim at Palestinian citizens of Israel who voted.
In a party statement shared by Netanyahu, it claimed the elections “were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences”. According to The Times of Israel, police and the Central Elections Committee have already dismissed these claims.
What the results show: Likud is on course for 26 seats, the largest party, with 20.65 percent of the vote. But his bloc has 53 seats, eight short of a majority.
Pre-election: In a September interview with The Jerusalem Post, he dismissed the idea he would need to form a coalition with Arab parties: “I believe the majority we receive will be much larger than what the polls currently show,” adding “I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles.”
He also said his “inner feeling is that I now have the ability to defeat Netanyahu”.
Election day: Eisenkot rallied Israelis to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”.
However, he acknowledged how tight the race was, saying, “We are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state.”
Post-election day: On Wednesday, Eisenkot told his supporters the Israeli public “voted against” Netanyahu and promised, “to ensure that the people’s decision is translated into a Zionist government”.
What the results show: Yashar is on course for 21 seats, with 16.16 percent. His bloc has 48, 13 short of a majority, and he cannot reach 61 without the Arab-led parties.
Pre-election: In February, months before the vote, Bennett told a closed conference of party activists that he stood by his 2021 decision to govern with Ra’am, but said he would not repeat it.
He said, “We will establish a unity government under my leadership … We are going to win, and we are going to form it,” Israel National News reported.
Election day: “Netanyahu has lost, and the October 7 government is going home,” Bennett told supporters in Tel Aviv.
Post-election: In a post on X, Bennett told Israelis to “lift your heads” and said he will do everything “to establish a Zionist Alliance of Servants government”.
What the results show: Together is on course for 12 seats with 9.07 percent, narrowly behind the Joint List.
Pre-election: In his election campaign, Ben-Gvir expressed his most genocidal views yet, saying in August that there are Palestinians in Gaza “who are not worthy of life. They shouldn’t live. They’re not even people.” He called for Israel to kill “30 to 40” people in Gaza every night.
Election day: “If you want this country to stay Jewish and Zionist, if you don’t want it to be in the hands of (Israeli Knesset members) Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi, go out and vote,” he told supporters at the entrance to the Arab city of Kafr Qasim.
What the results show: Otzma Yehudit is on course for seven seats, with 5.58 percent, less than half of the 15 he wanted.
Pre-election: In a statement he issued in August, he promised an expansion of his settlement “revolution” with a programme for the “Judaization of the Negev and the Galilee” at the expense of Palestinians, as part of his campaign.
Election day: He warned on Facebook of high turnout in communities of Palestinian citizens of Israel, claiming that failing to mobilise right-wing voters could let “terror supporters” into government.
That night, he told supporters “Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza.”
What the results show: Religious Zionism is on course for six seats, with 4.78 percent.
Pre-election: In August, he stated that only “a large and strong Joint List will work with all its might to send the Netanyahu/Ben-Gvir/Smotrich government home”, according to The Jerusalem Post.
Election day, night: In a video statement, he said Netanyahu knew “we can put an end to his bloody reign.”
Post-election: He wrote on X  that his party was ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”, which he called one of “bloodshed”.
“Against a politics of supremacy, racism, and exclusion, we offer a completely different alternative. The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote.
What the results show: The Joint List is on course for 12 seats with 9.14 percent, making it the third-largest party by vote share.
Election day, night: In July, Abbas set Ra’am a goal of at least seven seats, enough, he argued, to make it the balance of power in a “government of change”.
Election day: He hit back at Netanyahu’s posts about Palestinian citizens of Israel, stating in a video that he was “lying and inciting against Ra’am, using it as a scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters and drive them to the polls”.
What the results show: Ra’am is on course for eight seats, with 6.09 percent, beating his target of seven.
Pre-election: On October 15, he claimed: “We will reach 61 seats or more for the change bloc.”
Election day: He urged patience, saying on Friday, “we’ll be able to talk about a much better and more optimistic picture.”
What the results show: Yisrael Beiteinu is on course for seven seats, with 5.93 percent.
Pre-election: In September, he posted a statement which said, “Netanyahu ignored every warning before October 7, and now, 28 days before the election, he’s suddenly busy fear-mongering.”
Election day: He declared victory, stating, “The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat.”
What the results show: Together, which he co-leads with Bennett, is on course for 12 seats, with 9.07 percent.

articles.title_zh: ‘Catastrophic’: Medicare Part D changes could swallow your Social Security COLA raise
articles.content_orig:

Retirees will see a monthly bump of 3.6% on their Social Security retirement check starting in January, thanks to the annual cost-of-living (COLA) adjustment. On average, that translates to an extra $75 per month — the biggest bump in four years.
While that’s in line with inflation, will an extra $75 a month make a significant difference, especially for older Americans facing rising healthcare costs?
By signing up, you accept Moneywise Terms of Use , Subscription Agreement , and Privacy Policy .
Lorrie Ufkin, 71, told The Associated Press that the COLA increase “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare .”
By signing up, you accept Moneywise Terms of Use , Subscription Agreement , and Privacy Policy .
A temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program helped Americans like Ufkin offset their premiums over the past two years. But the Trump administration is ending that program early, wrapping it up by the end of the year.
For Ufkin, that’s “catastrophic.” Both she and her husband rely on a prescription that will jump from $11 per month to $200 per month. Combined, their monthly out-of-pocket costs will surge from $22 to $400 — completely swallowing their COLA increase.
Along with the rising cost of living — everything from gas to groceries to utilities — upcoming healthcare adjustments could deliver a serious blow to your bottom line.
Open enrollment for Medicare has already begun and runs until Dec. 7. During this window, you can review and update your health and prescription drug coverage. Changes will go into effect Jan. 1, 2027.
You can enroll in a standalone prescription drug plan (PDP) through Medicare Part D to supplement your traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage plan. Private insurance companies provide Part D plans with federal approval.
But a few major policy shifts could impact your choices for 2027:
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) says the average standalone Part D premiums will rise by less than $1 per month in 2027. The agency also estimates average Medicare Advantage premiums will fall more than 16%, while overall prescription drug premiums will drop 38%.
In part, that could be attributed to Medicare-negotiated prices for 15 drugs, which include weight-loss and diabetes medications.
But an independent analysis of CMS data by KFF, a nonprofit healthcare research organization, uncovered a more complicated issue. While many enrollees will see only modest premium changes, others face “ substantially higher premiums ” if they don’t switch plans. Enrollees also face a declining selection of standalone Plan D options.
Juliette Cubanski, deputy director of KFF’s Medicare policy program, wrote on X that raw CMS data fails to deliver.
“The data released today don’t tell us anything about plan changes underneath the hood to control costs,” she wrote . “Are plans dropping drugs from formularies, increasing copays, moving to coinsurance, etc. These features affect patient cost and access as much as (if not more than) premiums.”
Those changes to the fine print can “affect patient cost and access as much as (if not more than) premiums,” she added.
If you’re facing higher healthcare costs this year, shopping around is necessary so your costs don’t skyrocket.
AARP, an advocacy group for older Americans, is urging Medicare recipients to carefully review their coverage options before the open enrollment period.
“It’s more important than ever to shop around , compare your options, and choose the coverage that’s best for you,” said Nancy LeaMond, AARP’s executive vice-president and chief advocacy officer.
Here are some steps to take before Dec. 7:
“Medicare beneficiaries may want to evaluate what other features of their Part D plan might be changing, including what drugs are and aren’t covered on the plan’s formulary, tier placement of covered drugs, deductibles, and cost-sharing requirements,” according to the KFF analysis.

articles.title_orig: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.title_zh: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.content_orig:
We are announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory.
Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from the associated academic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies:
For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.
For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on.
For the physics result, form an external group of collaborators and defer to them on the release of materials.
We do not yet know which of these three approaches will be most useful, and we welcome feedback on what works and what we can improve.
The external collaborations will follow four principles:
Transparency. We are transparent about the existence of our collaborations. Participants will not be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements and will be free to discuss the work, share intermediate products, and publish their conclusions.
No Academic Credit. We do not seek academic credit for the discoveries produced by our internal models. Inviting a researcher to help steward a collaboration also does not imply that they or their working group made the original discovery.
Recognition. This group should receive recognition for the understanding they develop, the writeups they author, and the other materials they create. The group will also help ensure that the work appropriately credits researchers, techniques, and ideas that it draws on.
Independence. Participation is voluntary and unpaid. Working-group members participate independently, and their conclusions are their own. They do not speak on behalf of OpenAI, and OpenAI does not speak on their behalf.
We will turn over materials and artifacts related to these results to the collaborations. For the computer science collaboration, the group has decided to make the natural language proof and Lean formalization public immediately, and we are publishing them directly to our GitHub repository. For the physics collaboration, the group has decided to hold off on releasing the AI-produced artifacts and instead work on writing it up themselves.
All of these approaches involve tradeoffs. On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community. On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.
The result in mathematics concerns harmonic analysis. In 1991, Sogge proposed the local smoothing conjecture, which concerns the behavior of waves as they become focused. In particular, the conjecture states that the most extreme focusing must be short-lived. The amount of focusing at a typical random time is always much smaller than what can happen at the worst-case time. This is a familiar pattern throughout mathematics: what can happen in the worst case is more extreme than what is observed after averaging. Because of how fundamental this conjectured phenomenon is, it also has wide ranging implications throughout mathematical analysis. For instance, it implies the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture.
In 2019, Guth, Wang, and Zhang ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. In 2025, Wang and Zahl ⁠ (opens in a new window) proved the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. Our models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The new proof is based on a novel auxiliary partial differential equation.
We obtained our AI output on October 18th, 2026, which was formalized in Lean the following day, and then we reached out to an expert to discuss forming a collaboration around this result. Following their recommendation, we decided to release the AI output publicly, following the same strategy for this result as our October 6th, 2026 release ⁠ . We have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository.
The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. The ETH has been widely believed to be true, and has been used in hundreds of papers to derive conditional computational hardness results across a wide variety of fields including graph theory, computational biology, databases, computational geometry, and more. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research.
This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory.
Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and have authored a number ⁠ (opens in a new window) of influential ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) papers ⁠ (opens in a new window) on the topic ⁠ (opens in a new window) over the last 30 years.
Williams has refuted strong ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) versions ⁠ (opens in a new window) of the ETH, used ETH for hardness ⁠ (opens in a new window) ⁠ (opens in a new window) results ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and connected algorithms ⁠ (opens in a new window) and lower bounds ⁠ (opens in a new window) .
We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. The group invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research.
Our AI found its natural language disproof for the ETH on October 16th, 2026 and then subsequently we formalized the result in Lean on October 17th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. To that end, we have released both an AI natural language output writeup ⁠ (opens in a new window) produced by our models and a Lean proof ⁠ (opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository.
Computational complexity has many open questions and conjectures, whose proofs or refutations have so far eluded the best efforts of scientists. We hope that humans with AI can provide new understanding in this field, and shed light on the inherent capabilities and limits of efficient computation.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Ship on fire in Strait of Hormuz as Hegseth fires top general accused of leaking war info
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Ship on fire in Strait of Hormuz as Hegseth fires top general accused of leaking war info
articles.content_orig:
Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei seeking to restart peace negotiations, according to multiple reports, but President Trump insists it is a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he is still mulling whether to resume major military operations against Iran or make a peace deal after next week's midterm elections, according to various outlets.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Vance was engaging directly with Mohsen Rezaei, one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners, in an effort to revive negotiations, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.
Vance sent the letter to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' longest-serving former commander, at President Trump's direction, according to The Journal. The initiative seeks to establish whether Washington and Tehran can find common ground to avert a renewed conflict, the paper reported.
According to The New York Times , the letter, sent last week via Qatari mediators and delivered to Rezaei on Sunday, proposed an early meeting between American and Iranian officials, with Vance offering to lead the U.S. negotiating team.
The Times said Rezaei was expected to issue a formal response by Thursday. The letter did not specify a date or location for negotiations, but U.S. and Iranian officials were quoted by the newspaper as saying direct talks could begin as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey.
According to Axios , Vance's letter explicitly stated that any negotiations aimed at preventing new U.S. military strikes would require discussions on Iran's nuclear program.
Asked Wednesday about Vance's contact with Iranian officials, Mr. Trump told reporters he had not sought to renew peace talks, but "what that is, they [Iran] need help with medical supplies and various things. He [Vance] asked me what I thought and I said, 'If you want to do that that's okay.' Basically it's getting supplies in to help people who are not well."
An official briefed on the diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war.
A response is expected from Tehran by the end of the week, most likely Saturday, the official added.
On Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to transit what it described as "the unauthorized southern route" through the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy's public relations office said the incidents occurred over the past 24 hours, adding that the vessels were subsequently stranded along the southern shores of the strait.
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a southern shipping lane through the vital waterway, which President Trump himself declared mine-free at the end of August. Iran insists vessels can only transit the strait through routes it administers closer to its coast in the north of the strait, in coordination with Iranian authorities.
"These oil tankers had switched off all their radar and navigation systems," the IRGC added, referring to a common practice for vessels trying to avoid either U.S. or Iranian-imposed blockades in the strait and surrounding waters.
The vessels, "disregarding warnings from the IRGC Navy, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized southern route of the Strait of Hormuz when they struck naval mines and exploded," the IRGC said.
The IRGC said it held the vessels' owners and crews responsible for using the route that Tehran has warned against for months.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon official has told CBS News, after he was accused of leaking classified information related to the Iran war.
Sylvia was removed on Wednesday as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, becoming the latest in a series of generals to be ousted by Hegseth.
U.S. officials have told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections – as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter told the Associated Press.
President Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, stressed. He has, however, repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation have put the region on alert for a possible return to major operations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by Mr. Trump, but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.
The U.S. has told regional allies that a new round of military action could last for just several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate, which could bring longer-term fighting, the diplomats told the AP.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response would include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
The master of a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz reported seeing another vessel on fire nine nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, on Thursday, a monitoring agency run by the British military said.
The crew's status wasn't known and there was no damage assessment or report on the incident's environmental impact, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre added.
The strait is a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies. Since the start of the Middle East war in February, Iran has sought to control the waterway and has attacked ships it accuses of passing through the waterway without authorization.
The United States has responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the group at the kingdom's eastern region.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Saudi Arabia has this month come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years.
The Houthis said this week they had targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in the oil-rich Eastern Province with a ballistic missile.
Tehran has denied having anything to do with attacks by the Houthis after Saudi Arabia accused Iran of having encouraged the group's escalation against the kingdom.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said Wednesday the Iran-backed Lebanese movement was not concerned with the results of Israel's election , vowing to continue its "resistance" against the neighbouring country no matter who wins.
With 85% of ballots counted, the right-wing bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a slight lead over the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, but was still short of a majority after Tuesday's election.

articles.title_orig: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as Chief of European Central Bank
articles.title_zh: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as Chief of European Central Bank
articles.content_orig:
Departure of Lagarde, seen as candidate to take over World Economic Forum, comes as eurozone struggles with weak growth and inflation
Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, is stepping down nine months early, ending months of speculation about her future.
The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday morning that Lagarde would step down as its president on 7 February 2027; her term was scheduled to run until the end of October next year.
The ECB’s governing council thanked Lagarde warmly and gave her a longstanding ovation, as it met to set interest rates across the eurozone.
In a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a “great pride and huge privilege” to serve at the ECB.
“I think that I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” she added.
Lagarde has been seen as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct – which he denies.
Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.
“The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027,” said Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”
Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic . During her tenure the ECB has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war and the Middle East conflict and Donald Trump’s trade war.
after newsletter promotion
The ECB is widely expected to keep interest rates on hold on Thursday afternoon.
Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”.
She added: “Follow doctor’s orders and get your skin checked regularly.”

articles.title_orig: In Pompeii, a woman's wardrobe resurfaces with beauty items and jewels
articles.title_zh: In Pompeii, a woman's wardrobe resurfaces with beauty items and jewels
articles.content_orig:
The wardrobe of a woman from ancient Pompeii has come to light again. Thanks to the work of archaeologists it has been possible to recover the interior of a cabinet that held everyday items in house IX 11, 7, or the house of Cornelius Maximus, in the central area of the city buried by Vesuvius.
Looking at these objects, it is almost as if we can conjure up the life of a woman of Pompeii before the site was destroyed in AD 79. Among the finds are make-up tools(tweezers, a spatula for mixing pigments), a glass balsamarium, a perfume burner to fill the home with pleasant fragrances, a bronze lamp, alongside lead weights, probably used for a commercial activity and kept in a small wooden box of which only faint traces remain.
Vases and pots in bronze, glass and ceramic were also found: everyday household objects, but perhaps also heavy with memories, as in the case of an elegant little jug decorated with pine-scale motifs. There is also a necklace composed of at least 24 miniature objectsin faïence, bone, glass paste and rock crystal, all pierced for suspension and representing deities (Bes and Mercury can be identified), feet and hands, pine cones and bunches of grapes.
According to experts, such necklaces were sometimes regarded as "magical" objects used in spells and potions; in reality they are what are known as crepundia, literally 'rattles': necklaces with amulets that were given to children to protect them, but also so that they could be heard when they moved.
It was not unusual for adults to keep them too, often in small boxes or, as in this case, in cloth bags inside wardrobes, apparently as keepsakes of a childhood of which little else remained. The Roman world was characterised by a high degree of geographic mobility at all levels, from slaves to wealthy merchants, so that many people found themselves living far from relatives and parents and from the places of their childhood.
Another secret kept in the wardrobe unearthed in the excavation is a small hoard of coins: there are 38 of them, all bronze, preserved in a "cistella", a small container made of plant material using basketry techniques, the remains of which were analysed after being recovered during the dig. The presence of the coins in particular suggests that the owner or owners did not have time to recover the objects of value, whether economic or emotional.
If they were in the city at the time of the catastrophe, they will have tried to flee. If they managed to escape, they would not have returned to dig under the floors for their possessions, unlike others whose efforts have left traces revealed by recent excavations.
But perhaps they did not succeed and may be among those who, as the historian Tacitus recalls, died without heirs and whose property would have been used for the refounding of Pompeii, which ultimately never took place. These are questions destined to remain open.
"Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art; it is also somewhere where the most ordinary objects restore the human dimension of the past. The value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces of a life: personal habits, work, memories," says the director of the Archaeological Park, Gabriel Zuchtriegel.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of the person who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their everyday life," the director adds.
The excavation has helped clarify some aspects of the house in which the wardrobe was found. The facade of the dwelling, tentatively attributed to a figure named Cornelius Maximus on the basis of inscriptions now no longer visible, had already been excavated in 1912. Only now, however, has part of the rooms behind it been investigated, as part of the major restoration and accessibility project for the adjacent Insula dei Casti Amanti.
Although our knowledge of the house remains partial, some highly interesting data have emerged: on the one hand, the refined Fourth Style wall paintings in the room with the wardrobe, attributable to the workshop on Via di Castricio, indicate a certain standard of living, in line with the central position of the house, which overlooks one of the main arteries of the ancient city.
On the other hand, at the time of the eruption various works were nevertheless in progress that must have affected liveability considerably. Added to this is the discovery of at least two mouse skeletons, found inside an amphora on a mezzanine. According to analyses carried out in the park's laboratory, they probably belonged to the species Apodemus sylvaticus, also known as the "wood mouse".
Mice of this kind normally live in natural environments and gardens, from where they often invade attics and storage areas in human dwellings in search of food. The two specimens found at Pompeii were not fully mature, as indicated by the degree of development of their skeletons (117 tiny fragments). The discovery adds to evidence of the presence of rodents in other Vesuvian contexts, such as the service quarters of the suburban villa at Civita Giuliana or the sewers of Herculaneum, and offers the image of an urban society that also had to contend with unwelcome guests.
